---
title: Self-hosting
description: Run the masks server in production.
---

masks comes as a container image, `ghcr.io/masksrb/masks`. It runs on its own, or with a Postgres
server of yours. It migrates its databases each time it boots.

## One container

```sh
docker run --name masks -p 3000:3000 -v masks:/rails/storage ghcr.io/masksrb/masks
```

1. Run the command.
2. Find the setup token in the output. It is on a line like
   `masks: masks is not set up. Its setup token is 7Hq2…`.
3. Open `http://localhost:3000` and follow the **Set up** screen.

The container runs its own Postgres. Its data and the [master key](#the-master-key) live in the
`masks` volume, so the container can be removed and started again without losing anything.

masks answers plain HTTP only at `localhost`. To reach it from other computers, put a proxy that
serves HTTPS in front of it. This Compose file runs masks with Caddy, which gets the certificate:

```yaml
services:
  masks:
    image: ghcr.io/masksrb/masks:0.12.0
    volumes:
      - masks:/rails/storage
    logging:
      options:
        max-size: 10m
        max-file: "3"

  caddy:
    image: caddy:2-alpine
    command: caddy reverse-proxy --from auth.example.com --to masks:3000
    ports:
      - "443:443"
      - "80:80"
    volumes:
      - caddy:/data

volumes:
  masks:
  caddy:
```

Open `https://auth.example.com` first. masks keeps the address the **Set up** screen was opened at.
See [the public address](#the-public-address).

## What it runs

The image runs Puma, the web server, in front of Rails, on port 3000. It needs one Postgres server,
which holds three databases named from `POSTGRES_DATABASE`:

- the primary
- a cache
- a job queue

When `POSTGRES_HOST` is unset, the image runs Postgres 17 inside the container. It listens only on a
socket inside the container, and its files are in `/rails/storage/postgres`. When the server stops,
Postgres stops too.

- Background jobs, such as mail and retries, run in the web process by default. To move them to a
  second container that runs `bin/jobs`, set `MASKS_JOBS_IN_WEB_SERVER=false`. That needs a Postgres
  server of your own.
- The job queue stays bounded. A daily prune removes finished jobs after 7 days and failed jobs
  after 30 days. `MASKS_FINISHED_JOB_RETENTION` and `MASKS_FAILED_JOB_RETENTION` change those
  times, in seconds. A failed job is in `/up/jobs` and the logs until then.
- The web process also serves [LDAP](/build/ldap/) for apps that sign people in only over LDAP.

CI times a first sign-in on every push. It starts the image with the command above, waits for `/up`,
then creates the first manager and signs in. The seconds for each step are in the build job's
summary on GitHub Actions. `./dev first-sign-in` runs the same check on your computer against any
image, and fails when the whole thing takes longer than 120 seconds.

## Image tags

| Tag                            | Pushed on                                          | Platforms                                |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `:<version>`, such as `:0.12.0` | A server release.                                  | amd64, arm64                             |
| `:latest`                      | A server release. Moved to that release's version. | amd64, arm64                             |
| `:main`                        | Every push to main.                                | amd64, and arm64 too on a server release |
| `:sha-<commit>`                | Every push to main, named by the full commit hash. | amd64, and arm64 too on a server release |

Pin a version, as the examples do. Read
[CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/masksrb/masks/blob/main/server/CHANGELOG.md) before you move to a
new one.

## Your own Postgres

This Compose file runs masks with a Postgres server of its own and Caddy in front.

```yaml
services:
  masks:
    image: ghcr.io/masksrb/masks:0.12.0
    environment:
      POSTGRES_HOST: postgres
      POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ...
      POSTGRES_DATABASE: masks
    volumes:
      - masks:/rails/storage
    depends_on:
      - postgres
    logging:
      options:
        max-size: 10m
        max-file: "3"

  postgres:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ...
    volumes:
      - postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  caddy:
    image: caddy:2-alpine
    command: caddy reverse-proxy --from auth.example.com --to masks:3000
    ports:
      - "443:443"
      - "80:80"
    volumes:
      - caddy:/data

volumes:
  masks:
  postgres:
  caddy:
```

- `POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD` is the password of the `postgres` superuser. The entrypoint uses it to
  create the two [database roles](#database-roles) masks connects as, and to set their passwords.
  Use `POSTGRES_ADMIN_USER` for another role that can create roles.
- To create the roles yourself, leave `POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD` unset and set `POSTGRES_USER`,
  `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `MASKS_MIGRATION_USER`, and `MASKS_MIGRATION_PASSWORD`.
- The `logging` options cap the masks container's log, so a repeating fault cannot fill the disk.
- Every variable the server reads is in [ENV vars](/reference/environment/).

## The public address

The public address, or origin, is the scheme and host that apps and browsers use to reach masks. It
is the issuer, and every link in an email starts with it.

Without `MASKS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE`, masks learns the address from the **Set up** screen:

- Before setup, masks answers at any address.
- When the first account is created, masks keeps the address the screen was opened at.
- After that, masks answers only there and at the tenant's [custom domains](#custom-domains). Any
  other address gets a 404 that names the kept address.

To move masks to a new address, set `MASKS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE` to it, such as
`https://id.example.com`. The template wins over the kept address. To serve many tenants, each at
its own subdomain, use a template with `%{subdomain}`. See [tenants](#tenants).

### Health checks

A health check is a request that a container runtime or a monitor makes again and again to see if a
service works. masks answers two.

| Path       | Answers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/up`      | `up` while the server can reach its database, job queue, and cache, a worker has reported in the last 5 minutes, and no job has waited more than 10 minutes to start. Otherwise a 503 that starts with `down` and says which of those is wrong. `MASKS_WORKER_SILENCE` and `MASKS_QUEUE_WAIT` set the two times. |
| `/up/jobs` | `up` while no background job has failed in the last day. Otherwise a 503 that names the job classes that failed, and the tenants each one failed for on its last run.                                                                                                                                            |

- The image carries its own `HEALTHCHECK` on `/up`, so a container runtime such as Docker or Podman
  marks the container unhealthy when its worker stops. The example sets the same check for runtimes
  that read the Compose file instead.
- Point a monitor at `/up/jobs`. Leave it out of the container's health check, because restarting
  the server does not fix a failing job.
- A job that fails for one tenant carries on with the rest, records a `job.failed` event in the
  tenant it failed for, and is named by `/up/jobs` with that tenant.
- The errors themselves are in the logs.
- When a health check in the panel below is failing, `/up` adds a second line that names it, such
  as `failing checks: mail (demo)`. The status code does not change.

### The health panel

The overview in `/manage` has a **Health** panel. A job runs every check every 10 minutes and the
panel shows each result as a sentence, with what to do when something is wrong. **Check now** runs
them again.

| Check           | Looks at                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Background jobs | Whether a kind of job failed in the last day.                                                                                                                                                        |
| Worker          | Whether a worker has reported within `MASKS_WORKER_SILENCE`.                                                                                                                                         |
| Queue           | Whether a job has waited longer than `MASKS_QUEUE_WAIT` to start.                                                                                                                                    |
| LDAP            | Whether the directory answers without TLS to the network. See [LDAP](/build/ldap/).                                                                                                                 |
| Metrics         | Whether `MASKS_METRICS_TOKEN` is set and at least 24 characters long.                                                                                                                                |
| Mail            | Whether the tenant's SMTP server, or the one in `MASKS_SMTP_ADDRESS`, answers a connection. No mail is sent.                                                                                         |
| Public address  | Whether requests reach this tenant at its public address. A proxy that drops `X-Forwarded-Proto` shows up here.                                                                                      |
| Domains         | Whether every claimed domain still has its TXT record.                                                                                                                                               |
| Signing keys    | Whether the active key is older than the tenant's rotation period, missing, or left to rotate by hand.                                                                                               |
| Reverse proxy   | Whether forwarded headers came from an address outside `MASKS_TRUSTED_PROXIES`, whether a trusted proxy forwards plain HTTP, and whether every event in the last hour came from one private address. |

The first five are about the server and show the same result in every tenant. The rest are about
the tenant. A check that turns failing records a `health.failing` event, and `health.recovered` when
it is fine again.

#### A new release

Set `MASKS_RELEASE_CHECK` to `true` and masks reads the list of releases from GitHub once a day. When
a newer server release is out, the overview says so and links to its notes. The request carries this
server's version and nothing else, and nothing is sent without the variable.

A release whose notes have a line that starts with `Operator:` needs a step from you before or
after the upgrade. The overview says so, and the `release.available` event carries the flag.

## Database roles

masks keeps tenants apart with row-level security in Postgres. Row-level security is a rule on
each table that limits which rows a role can see. Two kinds of role can get around it:

- A superuser, or a role with `BYPASSRLS`, skips it.
- The role that owns a table can switch it off with one `ALTER TABLE`.

So masks connects as two roles.

| Role          | Variable               | Holds                                                                                    |
| ------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `masks_owner` | `MASKS_MIGRATION_USER` | The databases and every table in them. `CREATEDB`, and nothing else.                     |
| `masks`       | `POSTGRES_USER`        | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` on the tables, and the sequences behind them. |

On every boot, the image's entrypoint:

1. Creates both roles, and sets their passwords, when it runs its own Postgres or holds
   `POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. Their passwords are derived from the master key.
2. Runs `db:prepare` and `masks:grants` as the migration role.
3. Runs `masks:tenants`, which creates the declared tenants and prints the setup token of each one
   that is not set up yet.
4. Starts the server as the serving role.

Two checks stop a server that is set up wrong:

- The entrypoint refuses to start when `MASKS_MIGRATION_USER` is unset or names the serving role.
- The server refuses to answer a request while its role is a superuser, has `BYPASSRLS`, or owns a
  table that row-level security protects.

### Connection poolers

masks names the tenant on its Postgres connection with `set_config`, and row-level security reads
that name on every query. A pooler such as PgBouncer or PgCat keeps the name only in session mode,
where one client holds one server connection for as long as it is connected. In transaction mode,
each transaction may run on a different server connection, so the tenant named on one is missing
from the next, and a query would see no rows, or another tenant's rows.

The first time it enters a tenant, masks checks which mode it is in. It names a value on one
connection, uses another connection, and reads the value back. When the value is gone, masks refuses
to go on, with an error that begins "this server reaches Postgres through a pooler". Connect masks to
Postgres directly, or run the pooler in session mode.

Inside a transaction, masks names the tenant for that transaction only, so work you wrap in one
transaction is safe behind any pooler. A request is not one transaction, so this does not make
transaction mode safe.

## Encryption and secrets

For each tenant, the database holds accounts, sign-in factors, clients, tokens, signing keys, and
activity.

Columns that hold secrets are also encrypted with Active Record Encryption (AES-256-GCM). To read
them, someone needs the encryption keys as well as the database. These columns include:

- signing keys
- authenticator app secrets
- provider credentials and sending service credentials
- connected accounts' tokens
- event stream secrets

### The master key

On first boot, the image's entrypoint generates a master key and writes it to
`/rails/storage/master.key`. On every boot, it derives four secrets from that key:

- `SECRET_KEY_BASE` signs the session cookie. Anyone holding it can forge one.
- `ENCRYPTION_PRIMARY_KEY`, `ENCRYPTION_DETERMINISTIC_KEY`, and `ENCRYPTION_KEY_DERIVATION_SALT`
  make the keys for the encrypted columns.

What to know about the master key:

- Keep its path on a volume, as the [examples](#one-container) do.
- A secret set as an environment variable takes precedence over the derived one.
- To keep the key elsewhere, use `MASKS_MASTER_KEY` or `MASKS_MASTER_KEY_FILE`. See
  [ENV vars](/reference/environment/#required-in-production).

:::caution
Keep the master key with your database backups. Losing it makes every encrypted column unreadable,
permanently.
:::

Each tenant's encrypted columns use a key made from the master key and that tenant's own ID, so
nothing else needs backing up. See [tenant isolation](/build/security/#tenant-isolation).

### Running more than one replica

A replica is one of several copies of the server that share a database. Every replica needs the
same master key. Do one of these:

- Set `MASKS_MASTER_KEY` on each replica.
- Mount one file at `MASKS_MASTER_KEY_FILE` on all of them.

A replica that generates its own key cannot read the database's encrypted columns. It refuses to
start, with an error that says so. The same check stops a server whose database was restored with a
different key.

The tasks a server runs at boot, such as applying `MASKS_CONFIG`, running `MASKS_RECOVER`, and
re-encrypting after a key change, run once when several replicas start together. The first replica
takes a database lock and does the task. The others wait for it, see it was done, and skip it. Each
replica's log says which one did the task, so a recovery link is printed by one replica only. The
record lasts 10 minutes, so a replica that starts later runs the task again.

### Rotating the master key

1. Set `MASKS_PREVIOUS_MASTER_KEY` to the key in use now.
2. Put the new key in `MASKS_MASTER_KEY` or its file, and restart. At boot, masks re-encrypts every
   encrypted column with keys derived from the new one and prints that it is done.
3. Remove `MASKS_PREVIOUS_MASTER_KEY` and restart again.

A new `SECRET_KEY_BASE` comes with the new key, so everyone signs in again after the restart.

## Metrics

masks can report figures to Prometheus, a tool that collects numbers from services over time.

1. Set `MASKS_METRICS_TOKEN`.
2. Point Prometheus at `/metrics`, with that token as a bearer token:

   ```yaml
   scrape_configs:
     - job_name: masks
       authorization:
         credentials: the-value-of-MASKS_METRICS_TOKEN
       static_configs:
         - targets: [masks:3000]
   ```

Without the variable, `/metrics` answers 404. It answers 30 requests from each IP address each
minute.

The gauges count from the database on each scrape, so their figures agree across replicas.

| Metric                             | Counts                                                   |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `masks_tenants`                    | The tenants this server serves.                          |
| `masks_actors`                     | The tenant's accounts.                                   |
| `masks_sessions_live`              | The tenant's sessions that have not ended.               |
| `masks_sign_ins_last_hour`         | The tenant's sign-ins in the last hour.                  |
| `masks_sign_ins_refused_last_hour` | The tenant's refused sign-ins in the last hour.          |
| `masks_access_tokens_last_hour`    | The tenant's access tokens issued in the last hour.      |
| `masks_jobs_failed_last_day`       | The kinds of background job that failed in the last day. |
| `masks_jobs_waiting`               | The background jobs ready to run and not yet picked up.  |

The metrics that count something in a tenant carry a `tenant` label with its subdomain.

Two more metrics time the requests the process answered since it started. Each replica reports its
own figures, so scrape every replica.

| Metric                  | Reports                                                                                 |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `masks_request_seconds` | A histogram of how long each request took, from 5 milliseconds to 10 seconds, by route. |
| `masks_requests_total`  | The requests answered, by route and by status class: `2xx`, `3xx`, `4xx`, or `5xx`.     |

The `route` label is `authorize`, `token`, `userinfo`, `login`, `manage`, `discovery`, or `other`.
`authorize` covers `/authorize`, `/par`, and `/device_authorization`. `login` covers `/login` and
`/logout`. `discovery` covers the `.well-known` documents and the key set. `manage` covers the
console and its API. Scrapes of `/metrics` and `/up` are not counted.

## Backups, restores, and upgrades

Back up the primary database and the master key together.

- The primary holds every tenant's accounts, clients, signing keys, and activity.
- The cache and queue databases hold rate limits, replay records, and pending jobs. They can be
  recreated empty.

### Back up

In [one container](#one-container), dump the primary database from inside it:

```sh
docker exec masks pg_dump --host=/rails/tmp/postgres --format=custom masks_production > masks.dump
```

With your own Postgres:

1. Dump the primary database as a Postgres superuser. Row-level security stops every other role from
   reading all the rows, and the dump fails.

   ```sh
   pg_dump --username=postgres --format=custom --file=masks.dump masks
   ```

2. Keep `master.key`, or the value of `MASKS_MASTER_KEY`, beside the dump.

A dump restored without its key cannot be read, and the server refuses to start.

### Restore

Restore as the migration role, so the migration role owns every table again.

1. Stop the server.
2. Create the database as the migration role, and load the dump as it:

   ```sh
   createdb --username=masks_owner masks
   pg_restore --username=masks_owner --dbname=masks --no-owner masks.dump
   ```

3. Start the server with the same master key.

In [one container](#one-container), load the dump into the running container, then restart it:

```sh
docker exec -i masks pg_restore --host=/rails/tmp/postgres --dbname=masks_production \
  --clean --if-exists --no-owner --role=masks_owner < masks.dump
docker restart masks
```

Its first boot creates the cache and queue databases and grants the serving role what it needs.
Everyone keeps their passkeys and second factors. Sessions that were live at the time of the dump
work again.

### Upgrade

1. Take a backup. Migrations do not run backwards.
2. Read the release notes for anything that needs a step of your own. A line that starts with
   `Operator:` is one, and [the health panel](#the-health-panel) can tell you about it.
3. Change the image tag and restart.

Each boot runs the migrations that have not run yet, so you can skip versions.

With more than one replica:

1. Start one replica on the new image.
2. Wait for `/up`.
3. Replace the rest.

## Tenants

A tenant is a separate set of accounts, clients, and signing keys at its own subdomain. The
examples serve one tenant, `masks`. The image declares it when nothing else does.

To serve more tenants:

1. Set `MASKS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE` to a template with `%{subdomain}`, such as
   `https://%{subdomain}.auth.example.com`.
2. Name each tenant in `MASKS_TENANTS`, such as `acme,demo`. With `MASKS_TENANTS` unset, masks
   creates a tenant for each new subdomain that a request arrives at.
3. Point each host at the proxy. A wildcard host such as `*.auth.example.com` needs a DNS
   challenge, and a Caddy build with your DNS provider's module.

See [declaring tenants](/build/core-concepts/#declaring-tenants) for each mode, and
[setting a tenant up](/build/core-concepts/#setting-a-tenant-up) for the setup token.

## Custom domains

A tenant can also serve sign-in from a host of its own, such as `login.example.com`.

1. In `/manage`, open **Settings**, then the **General** tab, then **Domains**.
2. Claim `example.com`, and publish the TXT record it shows. masks checks the record every hour.
3. Point `login.example.com` at the server with a CNAME or an address record.
4. Under **Serve sign-in at**, enter the host and choose **Serve**. Only an owner can do this, and the
   host must be within a domain the tenant has proven.

What happens next:

- The tenant answers at both its usual address and the host.
- Each is a separate issuer, so an app names the one it uses.
- A passkey works only on the address it was made on.
- When the proof lapses or the domain is released, masks stops serving the host.

### Certificates on demand

Caddy can issue each custom host a certificate on demand. Before it issues one, it asks
`/tls/allowed?domain=`. That path answers 200 only for a custom host that a tenant serves.

1. Set `MASKS_ON_DEMAND_TLS=true` on the server. The path is closed until you do.
2. Point Caddy's `ask` at the server's own address:

```
{
  on_demand_tls {
    ask http://masks:3000/tls/allowed
  }
}

auth.example.com {
  reverse_proxy masks:3000
}

https:// {
  tls {
    on_demand
  }
  reverse_proxy masks:3000
}
```

## Declaring apps in a file

When a server's apps and groups live in a file, a rebuilt server comes back the same way. Mount the
file into the container and set `MASKS_CONFIG` to its path. Every boot applies it.

```yaml
name: Home
accent_color: "#3355aa"
password_reset_lifetime: 3600

groups:
  admins:
    name: Admins
    members: [ada]

apps:
  grafana:
    preset: grafana
    url: https://grafana.example.com
    client_secret_env: GRAFANA_CLIENT_SECRET
    allowed_groups: [admins]
  dash:
    preset: proxy
    url: https://dash.example.com
  wiki:
    redirect_uris: [https://wiki.example.com/oauth/callback]
    scopes: [openid, profile, email, groups]
    refresh_token_lifetime: 604800
```

|                                                                                                                     |                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`, `accent_color`                                                                                              | The tenant's name and color, as under **Branding** in `/manage`.                                                                                                  |
| `invitation_lifetime`, `organization_invitation_lifetime`, `password_reset_lifetime`, `email_verification_lifetime` | Seconds each [emailed link](/build/features/#link-lifetimes) stays valid, as under **Links** in `/manage`.                                                       |
| An app's key                                                                                                        | Its `client_id`, unless `client_id` names another. The app's own settings never have to change.                                                                   |
| `preset`, `url`, `slug`                                                                                             | A [known product](/build/features/#adding-a-known-app), as **Add client** registers it.                                                                          |
| `redirect_uris`, `scopes`                                                                                           | An app no preset covers. With neither `scopes` nor a preset, the app gets `openid profile email`.                                                                 |
| `name` under an app                                                                                                 | The app's name. Without it, masks uses the preset's name or the app's key.                                                                                        |
| `client_secret_env`                                                                                                 | The variable that holds the app's secret. Without it, masks makes a secret the first time and prints it to the logs once.                                         |
| `allowed_groups`, `access_token_lifetime`, `refresh_token_lifetime`, `refresh_token_absolute_lifetime`              | As on a client's **Access** and **General** tabs in `/manage`. Lifetimes are in seconds.                                                                          |
| `groups`                                                                                                            | Each group's name, and the nicknames or emails of its members. A member must already have an account.                                                             |
| `limits`                                                                                                            | Each [rate limit](/reference/environment/#rate-limits) by name, and its count. Applies to the whole server, so it sits at the top of the file, beside `tenants:`. |

- An app in the file is approved, and actors are not asked to consent to it.
- Applying the file adds and updates. It never removes an app, a group, or a member the file no
  longer names.
- A server with several tenants nests each one under `tenants:` by subdomain.
- A mistake stops the boot with an error that names the app or group it is in.

## Getting back into a locked account

Use this when nobody can sign in to reset an account. For example, the only manager lost their phone
and backup codes.

1. Name the account in `MASKS_RECOVER`:

   ```yaml
   environment:
     MASKS_RECOVER: masks/owner
   ```

2. Restart the server. At boot, masks removes that account's authenticator app, backup codes,
   passkeys, and sign-in codes. It signs the account out everywhere and prints a link to the logs:

   ```
   masks: masks: owner has no second factors now and every session is signed out. This link sets a new password once: https://auth.example.com/reset/...
   ```

3. Open the link and choose a password.
4. Sign in and set up a new second factor. masks requires one of every manager.
5. Remove `MASKS_RECOVER` and restart again. Every boot repeats the recovery while it is set.

Both the new password and the new second factor appear in the account's activity.

Without a tenant prefix, such as `owner` alone, masks finds the account in every tenant that has one
by that nickname or email.

## System requirements

masks has no fixed CPU or memory minimum. `RAILS_MAX_THREADS` sizes Puma's threads, and
`JOB_CONCURRENCY` sizes the background job workers. Raise either one if requests or jobs queue up.
See [processes](/reference/environment/#processes).

## Next steps

1. Read the tenant's setup token in the server's logs, open the tenant's address, and create the
   first account. See [setting a tenant up](/build/core-concepts/#setting-a-tenant-up).
2. Fetch the tenant's discovery document:

   ```sh
   curl https://auth.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration
   ```

   It confirms the tenant's issuer, keys, and public origin.

3. [Connect an app](/build/connecting-via-sdk/#connecting-an-app).
